items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Speech 'Deregulating in a Financial Boom: What Could Go Wrong?', 5th DC Finance Conference, American University, Washington, D.C.
items.quote: The bank deregulation undertaken so far, and the plans for more to come, is ultimately going to make our financial system less robust.
items.summary: Bank regulation and supervision speech. Barr argues that lowering large-bank capital and weakening supervision in a risk-on environment raises financial stability risk, and that unsafe practices at nonbanks should be regulated more. No statement on the policy rate path.
items.score_note: No monetary-policy content; official speech kept for coverage audit.

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Welcome remarks (pre-recorded video), State of Small Business Symposium, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland
items.quote: Achieving our dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices will create the conditions where small businesses and all Americans can thrive.
items.summary: Short welcome remarks on small businesses and the Fed Small Business Credit Survey. Only a generic reference to the dual mandate; nothing on the rate path.
items.score_note: No usable monetary-policy content; official speech kept for coverage audit.

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Speech 'Will Artificial Intelligence Broadly Raise Living Standards or Drive Income and Wealth Inequality?', Federal Reserve Board Financial Inclusion Conference, Washington, D.C.
items.quote: But future inequality will depend not only on what AI can do, but on what we choose to do with AI.
items.summary: Scenario speech on AI and income and wealth inequality (market concentration, labor substitution vs. augmentation, policy choices). No statement on inflation, rates or the balance sheet.
items.score_note: No monetary-policy content; official speech kept for coverage audit.

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Speech 'Economic Outlook', The Exchequer Club of Washington D.C.
items.quote: If we do not see signs of disinflation soon, I am prepared to act.
items.summary: Cook says inflation is 'simply too high' (PCE 3.7% in the 12 months through June) and that the balance of risks has shifted to inflation, citing the Middle East energy shock and AI-infrastructure capital spending as two unanticipated price shocks. She supported the June hold to give 'a bit more time' but sees risks 'strongly weighted toward higher inflation' and declines to predict the path.
items.score_note: Conditional readiness to hike while still endorsing the June hold: leans tighter, not an explicit call for a hike. AI is cited as a demand and price shock (capex), not as a financing or credit risk, so ai_financing is not tagged ('other' = AI capex demand).

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Speech 'Outlook for the U.S. and Alaskan Economies', Anchorage Economic Development Corporation 2026 Economic Luncheon, Anchorage, Alaska
items.quote: Still, I would support an increase, if it becomes necessary to bring inflation down.
items.summary: Cook says she is 'prepared to act by raising rates, if necessary' but that a hike may not be needed because three disinflationary forces are in play (tariff effects fading, oil expected lower, AI-related goods pressure easing). She explains her July vote to hold on that basis, and warns that after five years above target 'we do not have that luxury' of waiting long.
items.score_note: Explicitly open to a hike but conditional, and she says it may not be needed: +1 rather than +2. AI again cited as a demand and price shock, not financing ('other' = AI capex demand).

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Speech 'Unlocking Opportunities for Workers and Entrepreneurs with a Criminal Record', Second-Chance Lending Forum, Washington, D.C.
items.quote: However, if inflation appears not to be moderating sufficiently, then I think we should act decisively to raise rates.
items.summary: In a short outlook passage Barr says inflation 'remains too high' after shocks from tariffs, the Middle East conflict and the rapid AI buildout, with a risk of broader price pressures. Ahead of the September FOMC he sets a two-way condition: more time if data show inflation moderating toward 2 percent, a decisive hike if not.
items.score_note: Conditional two-way statement before the September meeting (more time vs. decisive hike): open to hiking with inflation risk dominating, not an unconditional call. AI buildout cited as a price shock, not financing ('other').

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Speech 'A Long-Term View on the Costs of Shelter', Housing Affordability 2026: A Community Development Summit, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago
items.quote: In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion.
items.summary: First remarks after the September 16 hike. Barr says he supported the increase because 'we were out of position', that inflation risks have increased while labor-market risks have receded, and that in his base case more adjustments are likely needed. The rest of the speech is on housing affordability.
items.score_note: Says further tightening is likely needed in his base case one week after a hike, which matches 'says more hikes are needed'. Hedged ('base case', 'likely', no timing), so a reader could argue +1.

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Speech 'An Update on AI and the Economy', Oakland Tech Week Opening Keynote, Oakland, California
items.quote: Looking ahead, I will consider what policy rate may be needed to continue to guide inflation down to our target.
items.summary: Cook says AI is adding inflationary pressure in the short term and postponing the return to 2 percent, with pressure broadening beyond the AI sector (electricity, water, core goods) and productivity relief not arriving in time. She backed the September 25bp hike, says the labor market 'appears to be well positioned to handle an increase in rates', and that the number and size of future adjustments depend on the data. She also says fighting sector-specific inflation with monetary policy could be a mistake.
items.score_note: Supports the hike and signals possible further adjustments, but data dependent and without a stated preference for another move: +1. AI is discussed as a demand and price channel (capex, wealth effect), not as financing risk, so ai_financing is not tagged ('other').

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Speech 'Economic Conditions and Monetary Policy', Detroit Economic Club, Detroit, Michigan
items.quote: In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion.
items.summary: Barr says inflation has been above target for five and a half years, that he does not yet see 'a clear trend toward a timely return to 2 percent', and that the AI buildout is having a measurable effect on prices on top of energy. He describes the September hike as a recalibration to balance risks and repeats that further adjustments are likely needed. He adds that a lasting AI productivity boost would imply a higher r* and a higher policy rate, and flags a possible repricing of AI investment as a growth risk.
items.score_note: Repeats that further tightening is likely needed in his base case, with 'What is clear right now is that inflation is too high'. Hedged wording ('base case', 'likely'), so +1 is arguable. AI repricing is mentioned as a growth risk but not tied to funding or debt, so ai_financing is not tagged.

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Speech 'The Dual Mandate in Rural America', 2026 Investing in Rural America Conference, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Asheville, North Carolina
items.quote: I am committed to returning inflation to our objective while preserving the strength in the labor market.
items.summary: Mostly about rural labor markets, inflation and small business. On policy Cook only repeats that inflation 'has been too high for too long', that it has exceeded target for more than five years, and that she voted for the September 25bp hike.
items.score_note: Thin policy content: restates support for the hike and that inflation is too high, no forward guidance. Scored +1 on the inflation-dominant framing; 0 is arguable.

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Conversation with New York Fed President John Williams at a New York Fed event (Fed calendar: Discussion 'Global Central Banking', Central Banking Seminar, virtual)
items.quote: The AI build outis potentially creating inflationary pressures that may not resolve very quickly
items.summary: Reuters reports Cook calling the AI buildout and its inflationary push one of her main concerns for 2027, and worrying about when productivity-driven disinflation will arrive and where the next supply bottlenecks will be. She said the conventional view was to look through supply shocks; Reuters paraphrases her as saying the optimal response could now be different.
items.score_note: Inflation-risk framing and openness to not looking through supply shocks, but no explicit rate call in the quoted words. Quote copied as printed on the page, including the 'outis' typo. No primary transcript found. AI cited as an inflation channel, not financing.

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Dissent at the October 27-28 FOMC meeting (FOMC statement, 10-2 vote to hold at 3-3/4 to 4 percent)
items.quote: Voting against the monetary policy action were Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack, who preferred to raise the target range for the federal funds rate
items.summary: The FOMC held the target range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent by a 10-2 vote. Cook and Cleveland Fed President Hammack dissented, preferring a 1/4 percentage point increase at this meeting. The statement gives no individual reasons; Cook explained her dissent in her November 20 Santiago speech.
items.score_note: Dissent in favor of a hike. The quote is the FOMC statement's wording, not Cook's own words (no separate dissent statement was published on federalreserve.gov). Drivers left empty because the statement gives no reasons.

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Speech 'American Inequality and the Future of AI', Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut (Fed calendar lists it as a virtual conversation)
items.quote: In my judgment, now is the time for society to begin to consider how to address these potential challenges
items.summary: Speech on the history of US income and wealth inequality and how AI market concentration and labor substitution could widen it. No statement on inflation, rates or the balance sheet.
items.score_note: No monetary-policy content; official speech kept for coverage audit.

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Speech 'Some Potential Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence', 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance, Milan, Italy
items.quote: However, with leverage at hedge funds and broader risk appetite apparently quite high, a sharp reversal could lead to rapid deleveraging and, potentially, self-reinforcing fire sales.
items.summary: Barr recaps the November Financial Stability Report on 'advanced computing debt': on-balance-sheet debt of the seven largest AI firms expected to exceed $800 billion by year end, off-balance-sheet obligations estimated above $3 trillion, more than $100 billion of circular equity financing, and weaker-credit firms shifting to complex asset-backed financings as their cost of capital rises. He says he is less concerned about direct losses given still-limited debt, but warns that hedge fund leverage and opacity could amplify a repricing. He also covers AI in trading, cyber risk, consumer finance and AI-agent-driven deposit runs. He says the Board does not target market levels and makes no comment on rates.
items.score_note: Financial-stability speech with no statement on the policy rate path, so score is null. ai_financing is tagged because he explicitly links financial-stability risk to debt financing of the data center buildout.
items.ai_quote: In the case of a significant repricing of AI investments, stress from these three aspects of AI financing could amplify the repricing of AI investments.

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Speech 'Investing in America's Underserved Communities', Making Missing Markets conference, Federal Reserve Bank of New York
items.quote: If the economy evolves as I currently forecast, I expect it will be appropriate to raise rates further to achieve that goal on behalf of the American people.
items.summary: In a short outlook passage Barr says the economy is strong with low unemployment and robust business investment, but inflation is too high and must come back to 2 percent 'in a timely way'. He expects further rate increases to be appropriate if the economy evolves as he forecasts, while continuing to watch the data. The rest of the speech is on community investment.
items.score_note: States that he expects further rate increases to be appropriate under his forecast, three weeks before the December meeting. No specific meeting named.

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Speech 'The U.S. Economy in Global Context', XXIX Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile, Santiago, Chile
items.quote: I am skeptical that September's single 1/4 point rate increase will be enough to change the path of inflation.
items.summary: Cook's first public explanation of her October dissent. Two reasons: financial conditions are too accommodative with no clear disinflation (the policy stance is not curtailing the AI buildout and equity prices support spending, so holding implies a widening positive output gap), and urgency after more than five and a half years above target, since waiting 'risks getting behind the curve' and could require larger hikes later that stress the financial system. PCE inflation was an estimated 3.8% and core 3.2% in October; data since September 'fail to provide' evidence of a return to a sustainable path.
items.score_note: Explains a dissent for a hike and says one hike is unlikely to be enough. ai_financing tag is a borderline call: she ties accommodative financial conditions and the policy stance to the AI buildout, but does not mention AI debt or credit explicitly.
items.ai_quote: The current stance of policy does not appear to be curtailing the AI buildout, and equity prices continue to support consumer spending.

coverage_notes: Sources checked: all 14 listed speech pages (opened and read), the Fed speech index and calendar JSON (federalreserve.gov/json/ne-speeches.json, /json/calendar.json), the press-release index, and the four FOMC statements in the window. The speech index shows no Barr or Cook speech beyond the 14 given, and no Barr or Cook testimony. Dissent check: June 17 statement 12-0 (no dissent); July 29 statement 9-3 (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan for a hike; Barr and Cook voted with the majority); September 16 statement 12-0 (25bp hike); October 28 statement 10-2 (Cook and Hammack for a hike). Barr did not dissent at any meeting in the window. No separate dissent statement by Cook is on federalreserve.gov; her public explanation is the November 20 Santiago speech (item included). No Reuters/Bloomberg coverage of the November 20 speech or any Q&A there was indexed yet when searched. Thin months: June (Barr: one unverified video-only chat and a regulation speech; Cook: welcome remarks only), August (only Cook on Aug 5; no Barr appearance on the Fed calendar), October (no Barr appearance at all; Cook only the Oct 1 conversation plus the dissent). This matches the Fed calendar, which lists no other Barr or Cook events in those months, so the gap looks real, not a search miss. No interviews (CNBC, Bloomberg, Reuters, podcasts) by either governor were found in the window. The Oct 1 Cook item rests on a Reuters article republished by The Star; the page has invisible zero-width characters inside some quotations, so the quote chosen is a stretch without them and keeps the page's 'outis' typo. Axios (2026-09-29, Cook AI inflation) and roic.ai pages returned 403 and were not used. time_et is null for speeches because the speech pages do not state a time. Scheduled times from the Fed calendar/speech index (ET), for reference: Barr 06-06 12:00; Cook 06-24 14:00; Barr 07-14 12:40; Cook 07-15 13:00; Cook 08-05 16:05; Barr 09-01 09:05; Barr 09-23 10:05; Cook 09-28 13:25; Barr 09-29 12:40; Cook 09-30 15:25; Cook 10-01 15:30; Barr 11-12 10:00; Barr 11-16 05:00; Barr 11-18 13:35; Cook 11-20 12:15. ai_financing was applied strictly: tagged for Barr 11-16 (data center debt) and, as a borderline call, Cook 11-20 (policy stance and financial conditions vs. the AI buildout). Cook 07-15, 08-05, 09-28, 10-01 and Barr 09-01, 09-29 cite the AI buildout only as a demand and price shock, coded as 'other'. Context check: nothing contradicts the brief. Statement pages confirm 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent through July, the September hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, and the October 10-2 hold; the FOMC calendar page shows the next meetings on December 8-9, 2026 and January 26-27, 2027.
